steps.say: Photosynthesis happens in the leaf, where a plant uses light energy to build sugar from simple ingredients.

items.text: Oxygen comes from the split water molecules

raw.topic: I was asked to prove the Pythagorean theorem: in a right triangle, the squares of the two legs add up to the square of the hypotenuse.
raw.title: Proving the Pythagorean Theorem by Areas

steps.say: We must show that in any right triangle, the two short sides squared add up to the longest side squared.

items.text: a and b = the legs, c = the hypotenuse (longest side)

steps.say: Construction: take four copies of this triangle and place them inside a big square whose side is a plus b, one in each corner.
The gap in the middle is a square with side c, because each of its sides is a hypotenuse and its corners are right angles.
First way to find the big square's area: its side is a plus b, so its area is a plus b, squared.

items.text: A = area of the big square

steps.say: Second way: add the pieces. Each triangle has area one half a times b, and the inner square has area c squared.

items.text: Each triangle: half of base b times height a

steps.say: Both ways give the same area A, so set them equal and subtract 2ab from both sides. What remains is the theorem.

question: How does the TCP three-way handshake work?

raw.topic: You asked me to explain how the TCP three-way handshake works, the exchange that sets up a connection between a client and a server.
raw.title: The TCP Three-Way Handshake

steps.say: Before any data moves, a client and a server use TCP to agree they are both ready, by swapping three short messages.

items.text: Server is already listening on a port

steps.say: Step one: the client sends a SYN message, saying it wants to connect and giving its starting sequence number.

items.text: Carries the client's initial sequence number, call it x

steps.say: Step two: the server answers with SYN-ACK, which accepts the request and also gives the server's own starting sequence number.

items.text: Acknowledges x+1 and carries the server's own number y

steps.say: Step three: the client sends an ACK, confirming it received the server's number, so both sides know the other can hear them.
Now both sides have agreed on sequence numbers and know the path works both ways, so the connection is established and data can flow.

raw.topic: You asked me to explain compound interest: interest that is earned on the money you started with and also on the interest already added.
raw.title: Compound Interest

steps.say: Money in an account, called the balance, earns interest each year.
With compound interest, the interest is added back into the balance, so the next year's interest is figured on a bigger amount.
The yearly rate sets how big each year's interest is, as a share of the balance.
After t years the balance is A = P(1+r)^t, where P is the start amount, r the yearly rate, and A the final amount.

items.text: A = final, P = start, r = rate, t = years

steps.say: Example: start with 1000 at 5%. Each year multiplies the balance by 1.05, giving 1050, then 1102.50, then about 1157.63 after three years (rounded).
Over time the compound curve bends upward and pulls away from simple interest, which adds the same 50 every year. After 10 years it reaches about 1628.89.

question: How does a neural network learn?

raw.topic: You asked how a neural network learns, so I will show how it improves its guesses by repeatedly measuring its error and adjusting its weights.
raw.title: How a Neural Network Learns

steps.say: Training data goes into the network, and the network turns it into a prediction using its current settings.

items.text: At the start, this guess is mostly wrong.

steps.say: The loss measures how far the prediction is from the correct answer, which is given by the label.

items.text: A big loss means a bad guess.

steps.say: Backpropagation works backward from the loss and produces a gradient for every weight, showing which direction reduces the error.

items.text: Each gradient says how the loss changes if one weight changes.

steps.say: Each weight w moves against its gradient, scaled by the learning rate η, a small step size, so the loss L goes down.

items.text: w' = updated weight, w = old weight, η = learning rate, L = loss

steps.say: The updated weights reshape the network, closing the loop. Repeating this over many examples steadily shrinks the loss.

raw.topic: You asked how binary search works: it finds a target in a sorted list by repeatedly checking the middle item and discarding half the list.
raw.title: How Binary Search Works

steps.say: Binary search needs a sorted list and a target value. Here we look for 11 in seven sorted numbers.
First it checks the middle item. Of the seven positions, counted from 0, the middle is position 3, which holds 7.
The middle value 7 is smaller than 11. Because the list is sorted, 11 can only be to the right, so the left half is discarded.
The remaining half becomes the new list, and its middle is checked. Of 9, 11, 13 the middle is 11, at position 5.

items.text: Same step again, on a list half as long.

steps.say: The middle value 11 equals the target, so the search stops and reports position 5. It took only two checks.

items.text: Each check halves the list, so it is very fast.

question: Supply and demand: how is a price set?

raw.topic: You asked me to explain supply and demand: how a price is set in a market by buyers and sellers.
raw.title: How Supply and Demand Set a Price

steps.say: In a market, a price is not decided by one person; buyers and sellers together settle it.
Buyers together form demand: the higher the price, the fewer units they want to buy.
Sellers together form supply: the higher the price, the more units they are willing to sell.
Where the curves cross, buyers want exactly what sellers offer: here the price is 8 dollars and the quantity is 4 units.
If the price sits above 8, say at 10, sellers offer more than buyers want, and that surplus pushes the price down.
If the price sits below 8, say at 4, buyers want more than sellers offer, and that shortage pushes the price up toward balance.

raw.topic: I was asked to explain Ohm's law, which says how voltage, current and resistance are linked in an electric circuit.
raw.title: Ohm's Law

steps.say: Ohm's law is about how much electric current flows when a voltage pushes on a conductor.

items.text: The push on the charges, measured in volts (V)
The flow of charge, measured in amperes (A)

steps.say: The conductor itself resists the flow. More resistance means less current for the same voltage.

items.text: How strongly the material opposes flow, in ohms (Ω)

steps.say: Ohm's law ties the three together: voltage equals current times resistance.
Example: a 12 volt battery across a 4 ohm resistor. Rearranging gives the current as voltage divided by resistance, which is exactly 3 amperes.

items.text: V = 12 V, R = 4 Ω, so I = 3 A

steps.say: Plotting voltage against current for this 4 ohm resistor gives a straight line through zero, and its slope is the resistance.

raw.topic: Recursion: a way of solving a problem where a function calls itself on a smaller version of the same problem.
raw.title: What is recursion?

steps.say: Recursion solves a problem by turning it into a smaller copy of the same problem.
A recursive solution needs a recursive case that repeats the step, and a base case that is simple enough to answer directly.
Factorial is a classic example: n factorial equals n times the factorial of n minus one, and zero factorial is one.

items.text: n = the whole number we want the factorial of

steps.say: To find 3 factorial, the calls go down: f(3) needs f(2), which needs f(1), which needs f(0), and f(0) is the base case.

items.text: f(0) stops the calls and returns 1

steps.say: Now the answers come back up: f(1) is 1 times 1, f(2) is 2 times 1, and f(3) is 3 times 2, which is 6.
Without a base case the function would call itself forever, so every recursion must shrink toward its base case.

items.text: Each call must move closer to the base case

raw.topic: You asked me to prove the Pythagorean theorem: in a right triangle, the squares on the two legs add up to the square on the hypotenuse.
raw.title: Proof of the Pythagorean Theorem

steps.say: Take a right triangle with legs a and b and hypotenuse c. We will prove that a squared plus b squared equals c squared.
Build a big square of side a plus b, and place four copies of the triangle inside it, one in each corner.
The four triangles leave a tilted square in the middle. Its side is the hypotenuse c, so its area is c squared.

items.text: A_inner = area of the tilted square

steps.say: Count the big square's area two ways: side squared, or four triangles of area ab/2 plus the inner square. Here a, b are legs.

items.text: Left side: side times side. Right side: pieces added.

steps.say: Expand the left side and simplify the right side. Both sides now contain the same term 2ab.
Subtract 2ab from both sides. What remains is a squared plus b squared equals c squared, which proves the theorem.

question: How does the TCP three-way handshake work?

raw.topic: You asked me to explain how the TCP three-way handshake works, the exchange that sets up a connection between a client and a server.
raw.title: The TCP Three-Way Handshake

steps.say: Before any data moves, TCP makes the two computers agree to talk, using three short messages called the three-way handshake.
Step one: the client sends a SYN message, saying it wants to connect and giving its starting sequence number.

items.text: SYN carries the client's starting number

steps.say: Step two: the server answers with SYN-ACK, confirming it got the request and giving its own starting sequence number.

items.text: ACK confirms client's number; SYN offers server's number

steps.say: Step three: the client sends an ACK, confirming it received the server's number.

items.text: Client now knows the server is reachable

steps.say: Now both sides know the other can send and receive, and both starting numbers are agreed, so the connection is established.
Only now does real data flow, and the agreed sequence numbers let each side order the bytes and spot any that are lost.

items.text: Sequence numbers keep bytes in order

raw.topic: You asked me to explain compound interest: interest that is earned on the original money and also on the interest already added.
raw.title: Compound Interest

steps.say: You start by putting in a first amount of money, called the principal, which becomes your balance.
After each period, the bank pays interest calculated on the whole balance, not only on the principal.

items.text: Paid as a percentage of the balance

steps.say: That interest is added to the balance, so the next interest is calculated on a larger amount. This loop is compounding.
The loop gives one formula: A = P(1+r)^t, where A is the final balance, P the principal, r the yearly rate, t the years.

items.text: A = balance, P = principal, r = yearly rate, t = years

steps.say: Example: 1000 at 10% a year. Year one pays 100, giving 1100; year two pays 110, giving 1210.
Plotted over time, the balance curves upward, because each year's interest is larger than the one before.

items.text: Growth speeds up as the balance grows

question: How does a neural network learn?

raw.topic: You asked me to explain how a neural network learns, meaning how it improves its answers from examples.
raw.title: How a Neural Network Learns

steps.say: A network learns by guessing from training examples, checking each guess, then nudging its inner numbers to guess better next time.
The prediction is compared with the correct answer, and the size of the mistake is a single number called the loss.

items.text: Small loss means a good guess.

steps.say: Backpropagation then works out the gradient: how much the loss would change if each weight changed a little.

items.text: Shows which way lowers the loss.

steps.say: Each weight takes a small step against its gradient, scaled by the learning rate.

items.text: w = weight, η = learning rate, L = loss

steps.say: The new weights change the network, which closes the loop. Repeating it many times drives the loss down toward a minimum.

items.text: Each pass moves the weight closer to the lowest loss.

raw.topic: Binary search: how it finds a target value in a sorted list by repeatedly halving the part still in play.
raw.title: How Binary Search Works

steps.say: Binary search takes a sorted list and a target, and finds the target without checking every item.
Each round it checks only the middle value. In our example the target is 11 and the middle value is 7.
Since 7 is smaller than 11, the target cannot be on the left, so that half is thrown away.
The search repeats on the kept half. Its middle value is 11.
The middle value 11 equals the target, so the search stops. Seven items needed only two checks, because each check halves the range.

question: Supply and demand: how is a price set?

raw.topic: You asked how supply and demand set a price, and I will show how buyers and sellers push a price until it settles.
raw.title: Supply and Demand: How a Price Is Set

steps.say: A price is shaped by two groups: buyers, who make up demand, and sellers, who make up supply.
Buyers want less as the price rises, and sellers offer more. The two curves cross at the price where both agree.
If the price is too high, say $10, buyers want 2 units but sellers offer 5, so unsold goods pile up as a surplus.
A surplus makes sellers cut prices to attract buyers, so the price falls back toward 8.
If the price is too low, say $4, buyers want 8 units but sellers offer only 2, creating a shortage.
A shortage lets sellers raise prices, because buyers compete for scarce goods, so the price climbs back toward 8.
These pushes stop at $8, where buyers want exactly what sellers offer. That balance is the equilibrium price.

raw.topic: I was asked to explain Ohm's law: how the voltage across a conductor, the current through it and its resistance are related.
raw.title: Ohm's Law: Voltage, Current and Resistance

steps.say: Ohm's law links three quantities in a circuit: the voltage pushing charge, the current that flows, and the resistance that holds it back.
Resistance is how strongly the material opposes the flow, so a larger resistance gives a smaller current for the same voltage.
Ohm's law states that voltage equals current times resistance, so current is voltage divided by resistance.
Example: a 9 volt battery across a 3 ohm resistor gives a current of 9 divided by 3, which is exactly 3 amperes.

items.text: Straight line: slope equals resistance, 3 Ω

steps.say: For a fixed resistor, voltage against current is a straight line, and its slope is the resistance; doubling the current doubles the voltage.

raw.topic: Recursion: a way of solving a problem where a function calls itself on a smaller version of the same problem.
raw.title: What is recursion?

steps.say: Recursion means solving a big problem by reducing it to a smaller copy of the same problem.

items.text: Same kind of problem, just smaller

steps.say: The shrinking must stop somewhere: the base case is a version so small that the answer is known directly.

items.text: Answer known without any further call

steps.say: Example: the factorial of n multiplies n by the factorial of the next smaller number, and 0! is defined as 1.

items.text: n = a whole number, n! = factorial of n

steps.say: To compute 4!, the function calls itself for 3!, then 2!, then 1!, and finally 0!, where it stops.
Now the answers flow back: 0! is 1, so 1! is 1, 2! is 2, 3! is 6, and 4! is 24.
Without a base case the calls would never stop, so every recursion needs a base case and a step toward it.

items.text: No base case means endless calls
